newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE-German bourse sees Telekom boost.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-German bourse sees Telekom boost.

text.p: The German bourse hopes that next week's sell-off of Deutsche Telekom, which will be worth some five percent of the DAX-30 index's value after it is sold, will help revolutionise equity investment in Germany.

"We have waited for you and are delighted to see your arrival. You are very welcome indeed," Werner Seifert, chief executive of Deutsche Boerse AG, said of Deutsche Telekom at the launch of a Telekom share roadshow in late October.
Telekom shares are due to be priced on November 16-17 and start trading in Frankfurt from November 18.

Seifert neatly summed up the view in Germany's investment community that Europe's largest-ever IPO will not only encourage small investors to buy shares, but also boost the German bourse, raising its profile among foreign investors.

"It's a definite boost. This is the third-biggest telecoms company in the world and it could make the breakthrough we all want and install an equity culture in Germany," said a Frankfurt options trader.
DAX CAPITALISATION SET TO JUMP
The total market capitalisation of the DAX index will increase by up to 75 billion marks, based on an initial price range of between 25 and 30 marks per share.
Deutsche Telekom shares were 12 percent above the higher end of the price range in the "grey market" early in the week at around 33.50 marks.
The grey market refers to the market provided by brokers prior to a formal offering, where shares are sold ahead of the IPO and honoured when it takes place.
On Monday, Telekom said it would increase the number of shares that it plans to offer to employees to 30 million from 20 million.

This move followed a decision by the company to raise its capital increase to three billion marks from 2.5 billion by topping up the initial public offer to 600 million shares from 500 million shares.
The IPO will represent around 23 percent of Telekom's equity and the share issue will be worth between 15 billion and 18 billion marks, Telekom said.
FUNDS READY TO POUNCE ON ISSUE
One London telecoms analyst said: "It has to be seen whether the private investors who invest in Telekom are there for the long-term or whether they take a big premium and run with it."
"However, even if you don't think the Telekom stock is worth anything, it will be driven by those who want to be neutral in the stock, which is still quite a lot of investors," said the analyst.
Fund managers are watching the situation, and the general consensus is that they will be buying the stock.
"All fund management companies are following the Telekom issue," said Rolf Passow, head of the association of German investment fund management companies, the BVI.
He added: "It depends what weighting the fund managers want to have, whether they are index-oriented or tracking something else, how the share does after flotation."
"But the fund managers will be there. It's positive because it has done a whole lot to get this word 'share' onto people's lips," said Passow.
MARKET BRACES FOR EARLY RUSH

A possible downside, some market players say, is that the DAX is oversold at the moment and that the worst impact the flotation could have is that it could push the index further into overvalued territory.

"The first day will definitely be interesting, as some will be profit-taking while others will be buying. The question is how much profit-taking goes on and what level. I think quite a few people will take profits early on," said the analyst.

Nearly twice as many shareholders have signed up for Telekom's IPO as Britons who registered for the British Telecom listing 12 years ago, the traditional benchmark for flotations in the telecommunications sector.

In expectation of the increased volume of trade on issue, the bourse will temporarily extend its floor trading session by one and a half hours to 1300 GMT and extend IBIS electronic share trade by two hours to 1700 GMT during the first week of trade after Telekom's IPO.

The bourse said that the extra trading hours have only been introduced to handle the massive extra volume expected from the Telekom flotation and are not part of a plan to extend German share trade hours.
